_about: Arm D public health and community vocabulary. Items are generated in the browser from these terms.
Three styles: 'define' (term -> pick the definition), 'name' (definition -> pick the term), 'apply' (vignette -> pick the term).
Distractors are drawn from other terms in the same category, preferring the ids listed in 'confusable', so every wrong answer is a real neighboring concept.
Definitions are written to a consistent length (roughly 12-24 words) and never contain the term itself; examples never name the term. The validator checks both.
Era: the literature cutoff of about 2016 applies. No COVID-19, no programs launched after the cutoff.

assessment.name: Community assessment
assessment.source: AAOS Community Health Paramedicine (2018); standard community health nursing usage

epi.name: Epidemiology and infection control
epi.source: CDC Principles of Epidemiology (3rd ed.); CDC infection control guidance

prevention.name: Prevention and screening
prevention.source: USPSTF; CDC; AAOS Community Health Paramedicine (2018)

behavior.name: Health behavior and education
behavior.source: Miller and Rollnick, Motivational Interviewing (3rd ed., 2013); Prochaska and DiClemente; AHRQ health literacy tools

sdoh.name: Social determinants and resources
sdoh.source: Healthy People 2020; WHO Commission on Social Determinants of Health (2008); AAOS Community Health Paramedicine (2018)

systems.name: Care coordination and health systems
systems.source: IHI Triple Aim (2008); CMS program definitions; AAOS Community Health Paramedicine (2018)

ethics.name: Ethics and legal
ethics.source: Beauchamp and Childress, Principles of Biomedical Ethics; HIPAA Privacy Rule; standard EMS legal usage

terms.definition: A first look at a community made by driving through it and recording what can be seen: housing, roads, businesses, people, hazards.
terms.example: Before her first shift in a new district, a paramedic drives every main street noting boarded storefronts, the one grocery store, and where older people gather.

terms.definition: An on-foot observation of a neighborhood that captures details a vehicle misses, such as sidewalks, stairs, lighting and conversations.
terms.example: Two program staff spend an afternoon on foot in the housing complex, counting broken step lights and talking with residents on their porches.

terms.definition: A structured conversation with a person whose role gives them special knowledge of a community, such as a pastor, pharmacist or school nurse.
terms.example: The program manager sits down with the long-serving pharmacist on Main Street to learn which patients struggle to afford refills.

terms.definition: A small, guided group discussion used to gather opinions and experiences on a defined topic from people who share a characteristic.
terms.example: Eight caregivers of people with dementia meet for ninety minutes with a facilitator to describe what makes hospital discharges go wrong.

terms.definition: An open public meeting where any resident can speak about local health concerns and priorities.
terms.example: The fire chief books the library hall, posts flyers, and invites anyone in town to come and say what worries them about health services.

terms.definition: A systematic process for identifying a population's health problems and the resources available to address them, used to set priorities.
terms.example: Over six months a hospital and the EMS agency compile hospitalization data, survey residents and interview clinic staff to decide which three problems to tackle first.

terms.definition: Cataloging a community's existing strengths, organizations and skills rather than its deficits, as a base for building programs.
terms.example: Instead of listing what the town lacks, the team lists its churches, the senior center, a retired nurse who volunteers, and a van the VFW owns.

terms.definition: A comparison of the services a population needs with the services actually available, to show where the shortfalls lie.
terms.example: The report lays two columns side by side: what discharged heart failure patients require in the first week, and what anyone in the county can currently provide.

terms.definition: Information collected firsthand for the current purpose, through surveys, interviews or direct observation.
terms.example: The program writes its own ten-question survey and hands it to every patient seen in March.

terms.definition: Information already collected by someone else for another purpose, such as census counts, hospital records or vital statistics.
terms.example: Rather than survey anyone, the analyst pulls five years of county emergency department visit counts from the state database.

terms.definition: Descriptive, non-numerical information about experiences, meanings and reasons, gathered through interviews, open questions or observation.
terms.example: The findings section is built from quotations: how patients describe waiting for a ride, what the word 'discharge' means to them.

terms.definition: Information expressed as numbers that can be counted, measured and compared, such as rates, counts and scores.
terms.example: The dashboard shows 212 fall calls last year, a 30-day readmission rate of 18 percent, and an average of 4.1 medications per patient.

terms.definition: Official records of births, deaths, marriages and causes of death compiled by government registries.
terms.example: The county health officer reports that deaths from falls in people over 80 have risen for three straight years, citing the state registry.

terms.definition: Learning about a group by taking part in its activities while systematically observing and recording what happens.
terms.example: A paramedic volunteers at the weekly food pantry for a month, working the line while noting who comes, when, and what they ask about.

terms.definition: Any person or organization with an interest in, influence over, or effect from a program's decisions and outcomes.
terms.example: The planning list includes the hospital, the county commissioners, the two clinics, the ambulance union, and the residents themselves.

terms.definition: A formal alliance of organizations and individuals that pool their resources toward a shared local health goal.
terms.example: The hospital, the health department, two churches and the EMS agency sign an agreement to jointly run the falls-prevention effort.

terms.definition: A maintained listing of local services, eligibility rules and contact details that clinicians use to connect patients with help.
terms.example: The binder in the vehicle lists every food pantry, transportation program and utility-assistance office in the county with hours and phone numbers.

terms.definition: The number of new cases of a condition arising in a population during a defined period of time.
terms.example: Last year 40 residents of the county were newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes.

terms.definition: The total number of existing cases of a condition in a population at a given point or over a period, new and old together.
terms.example: On the first of January, 1,900 of the county's 20,000 residents were living with diabetes.

terms.definition: The state of having a disease or the amount of illness in a population, as opposed to death from it.
terms.example: The report describes how much heart failure limits daily activity across the region, not how many it kills.

terms.definition: The number of deaths in a population during a period, usually expressed per 1,000 or 100,000 people.
terms.example: The state reports 850 deaths per 100,000 residents in the county last year, from all causes.

terms.definition: The proportion of people diagnosed with a specific disease who go on to die from it within a defined period.
terms.example: Of 200 people hospitalized with the illness during the outbreak, 6 died: three percent.

terms.definition: The proportion of an exposed group who develop illness during an outbreak, used to identify the source.
terms.example: Of 60 people who ate the potato salad at the picnic, 45 became ill; of 30 who did not, one did.

terms.definition: A disease that is constantly present in a given population or geographic area at its usual, expected level.
terms.example: Lyme disease turns up in the county every summer at roughly the same rate, and nobody is surprised by it.

terms.definition: An occurrence of a disease at a level clearly above what is normally expected in that population or area.
terms.example: The county usually sees ten cases of pertussis a year; by March there were ninety.

terms.definition: An epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents, affecting a large share of the world's population.
terms.example: The 2009 H1N1 influenza strain reached every continent within months of its first identification.

terms.definition: A sudden increase in cases of a disease in a limited place or group, more than expected for that setting.
terms.example: Twelve residents of one nursing home wing develop vomiting and diarrhea over a weekend.

terms.definition: A grouping of cases of a condition in a place or time that appears greater than expected, whether or not a cause is known.
terms.example: Three children on the same street are diagnosed with the same rare cancer within two years, and the health department is asked to look.

terms.definition: The ongoing, systematic collection, analysis and reporting of health data to guide action, such as tracking reportable diseases.
terms.example: Every laboratory in the state must report a positive tuberculosis culture to the health department within 24 hours.

terms.definition: The six linked elements a pathogen needs to spread: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, host.
terms.example: Hand hygiene works because it breaks one link; a vaccine works because it removes another.

terms.definition: The habitat in which an infectious agent normally lives, grows and multiplies, whether a person, animal or environment.
terms.example: Deer mice carrying hantavirus in their droppings are where the virus persists between human cases.

terms.definition: A living organism, usually an insect or arthropod, that carries an infectious agent from one host to another.
terms.example: The blacklegged tick carries the bacterium from mice to people.

terms.definition: An inanimate object, such as a doorknob, blood pressure cuff or bed rail, that can carry an infectious agent between people.
terms.example: The same pulse oximeter probe is used on six patients in a row without being wiped.

terms.definition: The way an infectious agent travels from its reservoir to a susceptible host: direct contact, droplet, airborne, vehicle or vector.
terms.example: Tuberculosis travels on tiny particles that stay suspended in room air; influenza travels on larger droplets that fall within a few feet.

terms.definition: Protection of unvaccinated individuals that occurs when a large enough share of a population is immune to interrupt transmission.
terms.example: A newborn too young for the measles vaccine is protected because nearly everyone around her has been immunized.

terms.definition: The process of making a person resistant to an infectious disease, usually by giving a vaccine.
terms.example: At the fall clinic the paramedic gives influenza shots to 60 homebound patients.

terms.definition: The minimum protective practices applied to every patient regardless of diagnosis: hand hygiene, gloves, safe sharps, respiratory etiquette.
terms.example: The paramedic cleans her hands and gloves up before touching any patient, whether or not anything infectious is suspected.

terms.definition: Additional protective measures, contact, droplet or airborne, used for patients known or suspected to carry particular infections.
terms.example: For the patient with suspected tuberculosis the crew adds fitted N95 respirators and keeps the vehicle ventilated.

terms.definition: Barriers worn by a worker, such as gloves, gowns, masks, respirators and eye shields, to block exposure to infectious material.
terms.example: Before entering the room she puts on a gown, gloves, a mask and a face shield.

terms.definition: A condition that laws require clinicians or laboratories to report to public health authorities when diagnosed.
terms.example: When the rapid test is positive for pertussis, the clinic must notify the health department by the next business day.

terms.definition: Actions taken to stop a disease or injury from ever occurring, such as vaccination, seat belts or tobacco-free programs.
terms.example: The program installs grab bars and removes loose rugs in the homes of older adults who have never fallen.

terms.definition: Detecting a disease early, before symptoms, so treatment can begin sooner, such as blood pressure checks or mammography.
terms.example: At every visit the paramedic checks blood pressure in adults who have never been told they have hypertension.

terms.definition: Reducing the impact of an established disease by managing it well and heading off complications, such as cardiac rehabilitation.
terms.example: A paramedic visits a man with heart failure weekly to review his weights, adjust his salt intake and keep him out of the hospital.

terms.definition: Enabling people to increase control over and improve their health through education, policy and supportive environments.
terms.example: The town adds sidewalks, starts a walking club, and puts fruit in the vending machines at the community center.

terms.definition: Planned learning experiences that give people the knowledge and skills to make informed decisions about their health.
terms.example: A class at the senior center covers how to read a nutrition label and what a serving size means.

terms.definition: Testing people who have no symptoms to identify those likely to have a condition, who then need a confirmatory test.
terms.example: Every adult over 50 at the health fair is offered a stool card for hidden blood.

terms.definition: A test performed in a person with symptoms or a positive screen to confirm or exclude a specific condition.
terms.example: After the stool card comes back positive, the patient is scheduled for a colonoscopy.

terms.definition: The proportion of people who truly have a condition whom a test correctly identifies as positive.
terms.example: Of 100 people with the disease, the new test picks up 95 of them.

terms.definition: The proportion of people who truly do not have a condition whom a test correctly identifies as negative.
terms.example: Of 100 healthy people, the test correctly clears 90 and wrongly flags 10.

terms.definition: The probability that a person with a positive test result actually has the condition, which falls as the condition becomes rarer.
terms.example: In a town where the disease is uncommon, most of the people who test positive turn out on follow-up not to have it.

terms.definition: An independent panel of experts that reviews evidence and issues graded recommendations on screening, counseling and prophylactic medications.
terms.example: The clinic follows the grade B recommendation to screen adults aged 50 to 75 for colorectal cancer.

terms.definition: A set of national ten-year objectives, issued by the federal government, for improving the health of all Americans.
terms.example: The program's grant application cites the national target for reducing hospitalizations from uncontrolled diabetes.

terms.term: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
terms.definition: The federal public health agency responsible for disease surveillance, outbreak response, immunization schedules and health guidance.
terms.example: The adult immunization schedule the program follows is published each year by the federal agency in Atlanta.

terms.definition: A federal toolkit for screening older adults for fall risk, assessing modifiable factors and intervening.
terms.example: The paramedic asks the three screening questions about falls, unsteadiness and fear of falling, then moves to the gait test.

terms.definition: A quick mobility test that times a person rising from a chair, walking three meters, turning, returning and sitting.
terms.example: It takes her sixteen seconds to get up, walk to the tape line and come back to the chair.

terms.definition: A structured check of a residence for hazards such as loose rugs, poor lighting, missing rails and unsafe bathrooms.
terms.example: With a checklist in hand the paramedic walks every room, testing the stair lights and looking under the bathmat.

terms.definition: Structured support that builds a person's skills and confidence to manage their own long-term condition day to day.
terms.example: Six weekly workshops teach people with arthritis and diabetes to set goals, solve problems and talk to their doctors.

terms.definition: Comparing every medication a patient is actually taking against the current prescribed list to find omissions, duplications and errors.
terms.example: On the kitchen table the paramedic lines up nine bottles, two of them the same drug under different names, against the discharge sheet.

terms.definition: The use of many medications by one person, often five or more, which raises the risk of interactions and adverse effects.
terms.example: The 82-year-old takes twelve prescriptions from four prescribers, plus three supplements.

terms.definition: A published list of medications that are potentially inappropriate for older adults because their risks usually outweigh their benefits.
terms.example: The paramedic flags the diphenhydramine and the long-acting benzodiazepine on the list for the provider to review.

terms.definition: A collaborative conversation style that strengthens a person's own reasons and commitment to change by exploring their ambivalence.
terms.example: Instead of telling him to quit, the paramedic asks what he likes about smoking and what he would gain from stopping.

terms.definition: Holding conflicting feelings about a change at the same time, wanting it and not wanting it, which is normal and not resistance.
terms.example: She says she really should check her sugars more, and in the same breath that it just reminds her she is sick.

terms.definition: A person's own statements favoring change, such as reasons, desires, abilities or commitment, which the interviewer draws out and reinforces.
terms.example: 'I'd like to be able to play with my grandkids without getting winded' is the sentence the paramedic reflects back and builds on.

terms.definition: A prompt that cannot be answered with yes or no and invites the person to explain, describe or elaborate.
terms.example: 'What does a normal day with your inhalers look like?' rather than 'Are you using your inhalers?'

terms.definition: Restating or paraphrasing what a person has said to show understanding and invite them to say more.
terms.example: 'So the pills make you feel dizzy in the morning, and that is when you skip them.'

terms.definition: A genuine statement recognizing a person's strengths, efforts or past successes, used to build confidence.
terms.example: 'You have kept every one of your dialysis appointments this year; that takes real organization.'

terms.definition: Responding to a person's pushback without arguing, by acknowledging it and shifting perspective rather than confronting it.
terms.example: When he says the doctors are all wrong about his salt, she says it sounds like he has thought about this a lot, and asks what he has noticed himself.

terms.definition: A model describing readiness to change as a sequence: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance, with relapse possible.
terms.example: The paramedic decides the man who has not thought about quitting needs a different conversation from the woman who bought patches last week.

terms.definition: The readiness stage in which a person is not considering change and may not see the behavior as a problem.
terms.example: 'My grandfather smoked till he was 90. I'm not worried about it.'

terms.definition: The readiness stage in which a person is weighing the pros and cons of a change but has not committed to act.
terms.example: 'I know I should walk more. I keep meaning to. Maybe when the weather turns.'

terms.definition: The readiness stage in which a person intends to act within the next month and is already taking small steps toward it.
terms.example: She has picked a quit date, told her daughter, and put the ashtrays in the garage.

terms.definition: The readiness stage in which a person has made a specific, observable change within roughly the past six months.
terms.example: He has been checking his blood sugar before breakfast every day for the past five weeks.

terms.definition: The readiness stage in which a change has been sustained for more than about six months and the focus is on preventing relapse.
terms.example: Two years after quitting, she still avoids the porch where she used to smoke after dinner.

terms.definition: A return to the earlier behavior after a period of change, treated in the model as a normal event to learn from, not a failure.
terms.example: After eight months without a cigarette he smoked through his brother's funeral week, and now wants to start again.

terms.definition: A person's belief in their own ability to carry out a specific behavior successfully, which strongly predicts whether they try.
terms.example: She knows exactly what a low-salt diet is; what she does not believe is that she could cook that way for her family.

terms.definition: A theory that people act on health when they see themselves as susceptible, see the condition as serious, and see benefits outweighing barriers.
terms.example: He gets the vaccine only after his neighbor is hospitalized with influenza: now it feels like it could happen to him.

terms.definition: Confirming understanding by asking a patient to explain in their own words what they have just been told, then re-teaching as needed.
terms.example: 'Just so I know I explained it well, can you tell me how you will take the new water pill tomorrow?'

terms.definition: A person's capacity to obtain, understand and use health information and services to make appropriate decisions.
terms.example: The discharge sheet says 'take with food twice daily as tolerated'; the patient reads at a fourth-grade level and takes it once at bedtime.

terms.definition: Communication written or spoken so the audience can find, understand and use it the first time: short sentences, common words, no jargon.
terms.example: The handout says 'weigh yourself every morning and call us if you gain three pounds' instead of 'monitor for fluid retention.'

terms.definition: A patient-education tool that encourages people to ask three questions: what is my main problem, what do I need to do, and why is it important.
terms.example: A poster in the clinic prompts patients to leave knowing their problem, their next step, and the reason for it.

terms.definition: An objective that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, so progress can be judged.
terms.example: 'Walk to the mailbox and back every morning for the next two weeks' rather than 'get more exercise.'

terms.definition: A short, written, patient-chosen plan stating what will be done, how much, when and how often, with a confidence rating.
terms.example: On the fridge is a card: 'I will check my feet every night after the news, 7 days this week. Confidence: 8 out of 10.'

terms.definition: A lifelong stance of self-reflection and openness to learning from patients about their culture, rather than claiming mastery of it.
terms.example: The paramedic asks the family how they usually make decisions about care, instead of assuming she already knows.

terms.definition: The ability of a provider or organization to deliver services that respect the beliefs, practices and needs of diverse patients.
terms.example: The agency trains staff on the dietary rules and fasting periods common in the neighborhoods it serves and stocks interpreter cards.

terms.definition: Unconscious attitudes or stereotypes that affect judgments and actions toward a group without the person intending it.
terms.example: Reviewing records, the medical director finds pain scores were documented less often for one group of patients, and nobody had noticed.

terms.definition: A trained professional, in person or by phone or video, who conveys medical communication accurately between languages.
terms.example: Rather than let the ten-year-old translate for his mother, the paramedic dials the language line.

terms.definition: The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age that shape health outcomes, such as income, housing, education and safety.
terms.example: Two patients have identical heart failure; one has a car, a stable apartment and a pension, the other has none of these, and their courses diverge.

terms.definition: A measurable difference in health outcomes between population groups that is linked to social or economic disadvantage.
terms.example: Amputation rates from diabetes in the county's poorest zip code are three times those across town.

terms.definition: The goal that everyone has a fair opportunity to reach their full health potential, which requires removing avoidable, unjust obstacles.
terms.example: The program sends the van to the neighborhood without a clinic, because equal hours at one site would not reach those residents.

terms.definition: Providing everyone the same resources or services regardless of need, which can leave existing gaps unchanged.
terms.example: Every household in the county receives the same mailed pamphlet, in English, whether or not anyone there can read it.

terms.definition: Action on the root social and environmental causes of poor health rather than on its later clinical consequences.
terms.example: Instead of treating more asthma attacks, the coalition pushes the landlord to remediate the mold in the apartment block.

terms.definition: A group at higher risk of poor health because of limited resources, social position or health status, such as frail elders or people who are homeless.
terms.example: The program prioritizes people over 80 living alone, those with serious mental illness, and families in the shelter.

terms.definition: A status in which leaving home takes considerable, taxing effort and another person or a device, used for home health eligibility.
terms.example: She can get to the car only with her son's help and a walker, and it leaves her exhausted for the rest of the day.

terms.definition: Limited or uncertain access to enough affordable, nutritious food because of a lack of money or other resources.
terms.example: By the last week of the month the refrigerator holds condiments and bread, and his blood sugars swing wildly.

terms.definition: Difficulty paying rent, overcrowding, frequent moves, or staying with others because of lack of a stable home.
terms.example: The patient has moved three times in a year and gives the pharmacy a different address each time, so refills keep missing him.

terms.definition: Lack of a reliable, affordable way to travel to appointments, pharmacies or food, which leads to missed care.
terms.example: The nearest dialysis unit is 40 miles away, the bus runs twice a day, and she has missed four sessions this quarter.

terms.definition: The physical, emotional and financial strain experienced by a person providing ongoing care to a family member or friend.
terms.example: The daughter has not slept through the night in a year, has quit her job, and cries when asked how she is doing.

terms.definition: Short-term substitute care for a dependent person, arranged so their regular caregiver can have temporary relief.
terms.example: For one weekend a month a home aide stays with her father so she can leave the house.

terms.definition: An objective lack of social contacts and participation, linked to worse health outcomes and mortality in older adults.
terms.example: He has not had a visitor in three weeks, the phone rings only for telemarketers, and the paramedic is the first person he has spoken to since Sunday.

terms.definition: The basic self-care tasks of everyday life: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence and feeding.
terms.example: She can feed herself and get to the toilet, but needs help getting into the tub and buttoning her blouse.

terms.definition: Complex tasks needed to live independently: managing medications and money, shopping, cooking, housework, transportation and using the phone.
terms.example: He dresses and bathes himself fine, but his bills are unpaid, the pillbox is a jumble, and there is no food in the house.

terms.definition: A state of reduced physiological reserve and resistance to stressors, marked by weakness, slowness, low activity, exhaustion and weight loss.
terms.example: A minor urinary infection puts the 88-year-old in bed for a week and she never regains her previous walking distance.

terms.definition: A joint federal and state program that pays for health care for people with low income, with eligibility rules set by each state.
terms.example: The single mother's children are covered through the state program, and she qualified herself after the expansion.

terms.definition: The federal health insurance program for people aged 65 and over and some younger people with disabilities or end-stage renal disease.
terms.example: At 65 he stops paying for the marketplace plan and receives his red, white and blue card.

terms.definition: A person who qualifies for both the federal program for older and disabled people and the state program for people with low income.
terms.example: The 72-year-old on a small pension has both cards, and the state program pays her premiums and copays.

terms.definition: A model in which paramedics work in expanded, non-emergency roles to fill gaps in local health care, such as home visits and chronic disease support.
terms.example: Between emergency calls the paramedic follows a caseload of 30 patients recently discharged with heart failure and COPD.

terms.definition: Patient-centered, mobile health services delivered in the community by a coordinated team that may include paramedics, nurses and social workers.
terms.example: The agency's program pairs a paramedic with a social worker and a nurse practitioner who share one list of patients and one care plan.

terms.definition: Deliberately organizing a patient's care among all the people involved so that information is shared and services do not conflict or fall through.
terms.example: The paramedic makes sure the cardiologist, the primary provider and the home health nurse all know the diuretic dose was changed on Tuesday.

terms.definition: A collaborative process of assessing, planning, arranging and monitoring services to meet an individual's health and social needs over time.
terms.example: One nurse holds responsibility for the man's whole plan: appointments, equipment, benefits, and the weekly check-in call.

terms.definition: Helping an individual overcome barriers to timely care by guiding them through the health system, appointments, paperwork and follow-up.
terms.example: The navigator books the imaging, arranges the ride, explains the forms, and calls the day before to confirm.

terms.definition: The movement of a patient between settings or providers, such as hospital to home, where information and responsibility are most often lost.
terms.example: In the 48 hours after the man leaves the hospital, nobody has told his pharmacy the dose changed and nobody owns his pending culture.

terms.definition: The process, begun early in a hospital stay, of preparing a patient and their supports for what happens after they leave.
terms.example: On day two of the admission the team asks who will be at home, who will fill the prescriptions, and how he will get to follow-up.

terms.definition: A transfer of care performed in person or in real time, in front of the patient, between two providers, rather than by a note alone.
terms.example: Before leaving, the paramedic calls the home health nurse on speaker with the patient present and walks through today's findings together.

terms.definition: A handoff to another service in which the sender is told whether the patient was actually seen and what happened.
terms.example: Two weeks after sending the woman to the food bank, the paramedic receives confirmation that she enrolled and picked up her first box.

terms.definition: A written, shared document stating a patient's problems, goals, planned interventions and who is responsible for each.
terms.example: One page in the chart lists his three problems, the target weight, the medication schedule, and the names next to each task.

terms.definition: A group of professionals from different fields who share goals and decision-making for the same patients, rather than working in parallel.
terms.example: Every Thursday the paramedic, a pharmacist, a social worker and a nurse practitioner sit at one table and go through the same 20 names.

terms.definition: A primary care model in which one practice coordinates comprehensive, accessible, team-based care for a patient over time.
terms.example: Her clinic answers the phone after hours, tracks her referrals, and knows what the specialist said before she does.

terms.definition: A group of providers that jointly takes responsibility for the quality and total cost of care for a defined population and shares in any savings.
terms.example: The hospital, its physician group and a home health agency are paid partly on whether their 15,000 assigned patients stay healthier for less.

terms.definition: A federal program that reduces payments to hospitals where more patients than expected return within 30 days for specified conditions.
terms.example: Because too many heart failure patients came back within a month, the hospital's payments were cut and it funded a paramedic follow-up program.

terms.definition: An unplanned return to inpatient care within thirty days of discharge, used as a marker of care quality and transitions.
terms.example: Discharged on the 3rd with pneumonia, he is back on the 19th with the same problem, and it counts against the hospital.

terms.definition: A framework for improving health systems by pursuing three goals at once: better patient experience, better population health, and lower per-capita cost.
terms.example: The program's annual report is organized in three sections: satisfaction scores, hospitalization rates, and cost per enrolled patient.

terms.definition: The health outcomes of a defined group of people and the distribution of those outcomes within the group, including their determinants.
terms.example: The health system tracks blood pressure control across all 40,000 of its attributed patients, not just those who come in.

terms.definition: Organized efforts of society to prevent disease, prolong life and promote health for whole communities rather than individual patients.
terms.example: Clean water, restaurant inspections, vaccination programs and seat-belt laws are its work; treating one patient's pneumonia is not.

terms.definition: The three foundational responsibilities of public health agencies: assessment, policy development and assurance.
terms.example: The health department measures the problem, writes the rule, and then checks that the rule is being followed.

terms.definition: A framework listing the activities every community's public health system should carry out, from monitoring health status to evaluating services.
terms.example: The accreditation reviewers check the department against the list: does it monitor, diagnose, inform, mobilize, develop policy, enforce, link, assure, evaluate and research.

terms.definition: Skilled nursing, therapy or aide services provided in a person's home under a physician's plan of care, usually after illness or hospitalization.
terms.example: A nurse visits three times a week to manage the wound and adjust the insulin under the doctor's orders.

terms.definition: Non-medical help with daily living in a person's home, such as bathing, meals, cleaning and companionship, without a clinical plan of care.
terms.example: An aide comes each morning to help him shower, make breakfast and tidy the kitchen.

terms.definition: Comfort-focused care for people expected to live six months or less who have chosen to stop treatment aimed at cure.
terms.example: He has stopped chemotherapy, a team manages his pain at home, and his wife has a number to call at 3 am.

terms.definition: Specialized care focused on relieving the symptoms and stress of serious illness at any stage, alongside treatment aimed at the disease.
terms.example: While she continues dialysis, a separate team helps with her breathlessness, her sleep and the conversation about what she wants.

terms.definition: A licensed setting providing 24-hour nursing care and rehabilitation services, most often after a hospital stay.
terms.example: After her hip surgery she spends three weeks in a unit with nurses around the clock and daily physical therapy before going home.

terms.definition: A residential setting offering housing, meals and help with daily activities for people who do not need continuous nursing care.
terms.example: He has his own apartment, eats in a shared dining room, and a staff member reminds him about his pills each morning.

terms.definition: Physician oversight of the clinical care delivered by EMS or community paramedics, through protocols, orders and quality review.
terms.example: Every dose adjustment the paramedic recommends goes through the program's physician, who also reviews a sample of charts each month.

terms.definition: The range of activities a licensed or certified provider is legally permitted to perform, set by state law and regulation.
terms.example: The state allows the paramedic to draw labs and give scheduled medications at home but not to start or change a prescription.

terms.definition: A written set of standing orders and decision rules, approved by a medical director, that guides a provider's actions in defined situations.
terms.example: The binder says exactly what to do when an INR is between 4.5 and 9 with no bleeding: hold, call, recheck within 48 hours.

terms.definition: A systematic, continuous approach to measuring performance and making changes that lead to better outcomes.
terms.example: The program tracks how many discharged patients are seen within 48 hours, sets a target, and changes its scheduling until it hits it.

terms.definition: A four-step method for testing a change on a small scale, measuring the result, and deciding whether to adopt, adapt or abandon it.
terms.example: For two weeks one crew tries calling patients the evening before visits; the no-show rate is compared, and the practice is rolled out.

terms.definition: A structured investigation of an adverse event that looks past the immediate error to the underlying system factors that allowed it.
terms.example: The missed pending culture is traced not to one paramedic but to a discharge template with no field for who owns outstanding results.

terms.definition: Making clinical decisions by integrating the best available research with clinical expertise and the patient's values.
terms.example: The falls program adopts the screening tool with the strongest trial data rather than the one the director used at her last job.

terms.definition: The ethical principle that a person with capacity has the right to make their own decisions about their care, including refusing it.
terms.example: The man understands he may die at home without dialysis and chooses that anyway; the team respects it.

terms.definition: The ethical duty to act for the benefit of the patient and to actively promote their well-being and interests.
terms.example: The paramedic stays an extra twenty minutes to set up the pill organizer because it will keep the patient safer.

terms.definition: The ethical duty to avoid causing harm, including the harm that comes from unnecessary treatment or transport.
terms.example: She declines to give the antibiotic the family is demanding for a positive dipstick in a patient with no symptoms.

terms.definition: The ethical principle of fairness in the distribution of care and resources, treating like cases alike.
terms.example: The program enrolls patients by clinical need, not by which neighborhood complains loudest.

terms.definition: A patient's voluntary agreement to a treatment after understanding its nature, benefits, risks and alternatives.
terms.example: Before drawing blood the paramedic explains what will be tested, why, and what happens with the result, and the patient agrees.

terms.definition: A patient's decision to decline recommended care after being told the risks of declining, documented with the patient's understanding.
terms.example: He declines transport for his chest pain; the paramedic documents that he can repeat back the risk of death and still says no.

terms.definition: A clinical judgment that a person can understand information, appreciate its consequences, reason about options and communicate a choice.
terms.example: The woman with mild dementia explains why she prefers to stay home and what could go wrong; the paramedic judges she can decide this.

terms.definition: A legal determination, made by a court, about a person's ability to manage their own affairs; presumed present unless ruled otherwise.
terms.example: A judge has declared him unable to manage his finances and appointed his daughter to do so.

terms.definition: A court-ordered arrangement giving one person legal authority to make decisions for another who has been found unable to.
terms.example: After the hearing, his niece signs the consent forms for the placement because the court gave her that authority.

terms.definition: A person named in advance by a patient to make medical decisions on their behalf if they lose the ability to decide.
terms.example: Years ago she signed a form naming her son; now that she cannot speak, the doctors ask him.

terms.definition: A written statement of a person's wishes about future medical care, prepared while they still have capacity.
terms.example: The document in her file says she does not want a feeding tube or a ventilator if she cannot recover.

terms.definition: A signed medical order set, portable across settings, translating a seriously ill patient's treatment wishes into actionable orders.
terms.example: The bright form on the refrigerator, signed by her physician, tells the crew exactly which treatments she has chosen and which she has declined.

terms.definition: A physician's order stating that CPR is not to be attempted if the patient's heart or breathing stops.
terms.example: When he collapses, the crew confirms the valid signed order and does not begin compressions.

terms.definition: The ethical and legal obligation not to disclose a patient's information to anyone not involved in their care without permission.
terms.example: The neighbor asks how the patient is doing; the paramedic says only that she is glad to see him and cannot discuss it.

terms.definition: A federal regulation setting national standards for protecting identifiable health information and for when it may be shared.
terms.example: The program signs an agreement with the hospital so that discharge summaries can lawfully be sent to the paramedic.

terms.definition: The rule that when health information is shared, only the amount needed for the specific purpose should be disclosed.
terms.example: The transport company needs the pickup address and the mobility limits, not the diagnosis list, and that is all it gets.

terms.definition: A legal requirement that certain professionals report suspected abuse, neglect or specified conditions to the authorities.
terms.example: Seeing the unexplained bruises and the empty refrigerator, the paramedic calls the adult protective services line that day.

terms.definition: Harm or risk to an older adult caused by the acts or omissions of a caregiver or trusted person, in physical, financial or emotional form.
terms.example: The grandson has moved in, controls her bank card, and she flinches when he raises his voice.

terms.definition: Failure by a responsible caregiver to provide the food, shelter, medical care or protection a dependent person needs.
terms.example: The bedbound man has a pressure ulcer to the bone, soiled sheets, and a daughter who says she has been too busy.

terms.definition: A person's own failure to meet their basic needs for food, hygiene, medication or safety, often linked to illness or cognitive decline.
terms.example: She lives alone amid stacked newspapers and spoiled food, has stopped bathing, and insists she is fine.

terms.definition: A legal obligation, arising from a provider's role or an established relationship, to provide care when it is required.
terms.example: Once the paramedic has begun assessing the patient, she cannot simply leave because her shift is ending.

terms.definition: Ending a provider-patient relationship without the patient's agreement and without transferring care to someone of equal or greater ability.
terms.example: The crew leaves the confused patient alone at home after telling him someone will 'probably' call tomorrow.

terms.definition: A failure to meet the standard of care that results in harm, requiring a duty, a breach, damages and causation.
terms.example: The paramedic documents a potassium of 6.8 with peaked T waves, leaves the patient at home, and he arrests that night.

terms.definition: The level of care a reasonably prudent provider with similar training would deliver in similar circumstances.
terms.example: The question in the review is whether another community paramedic, seeing the same INR and the same head bruise, would have transported.

terms.definition: A person's right to control who has access to their body, their physical space and their personal information.
terms.example: Before examining her abdomen, the paramedic asks the visiting relatives to step into the hall.
